highlights.rationale: The four printed sentences of *"Proof of 1.2, assuming 1.3"* (printed p. 4 = PDF p. 6), packaged as the standalone statement *no graph on a finite vertex type is a minimum imperfect graph*. The Lean proof follows the printed sentences one for one, in order: E5 gives Berge and not perfect, E4 gives not basic, E2 (Cornuéjols–Cunningham [13]) rules out a proper 2-join in `G` and, via 1.1 (Lovász), in `Gᶜ`, E3 (Chvátal–Sbihi [7]) rules out a proper homogeneous pair, 1.5 rules out a balanced skew partition, and 1.3 is then contradicted.
highlights.prose: Suppose that there is a minimum imperfect graph G. Thus G is Berge and not perfect. Every basic graph is perfect, and so G is not basic. It is shown in [13] that G does not admit a proper 2-join.

highlights.rationale: The Strong Perfect Graph Theorem itself, statement 1.2 of the paper, and the main result of this development: for every graph on a finite vertex type, `IsPerfect G ↔ Berge G`. The Lean statement quantifies over all graphs with no further hypothesis, exactly as printed, and is proved sorry-free (axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`). The forward direction is the paper's *"It is easy to see that every perfect graph is Berge"* (external result E5); the converse is obtained from `no_minimumImperfect` by passing to a minimum counterexample, which is the paper's *"a counterexample to 1.2 with as few vertices as possible"*.
highlights.prose: A graph is perfect if and only if it is Berge.

highlights.rationale: External result cited by the paper, not proved in it: G. A. Dirac, *A property of 4-chromatic graphs and some remarks on critical graphs*, J. London Math. Soc. 27 (1952) 85–92 — every finite simple graph of minimum degree at least 3 contains a subdivision of K₄ as a subgraph. The paper invokes it without proof in the opening sentence of the proof of 5.3 (quoted). NOTE ON THE ARTIFACT: this module is filed under `PriorWork/`, but the declaration is no longer an `axiom` — it is a `theorem` with a complete Lean proof (via `ProofLemmas.DiracK4SubdivisionInduction` and `ProofLemmas.SubdivisionDatumRealize`, both sorry-free), so the result is discharged here rather than assumed. `Nonempty U` is a genuine hypothesis: on the empty vertex type the degree condition is vacuous but no subgraph can carry an injection `Fin 4 → S.verts`.

erratum.problem: Theorem 2.5 (p. 10) is stated for a set X with no anticonnectedness assumption, unlike 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.10, which all require it. Without that hypothesis the theorem is false. Take 7 vertices with X = {x₁, x₂} adjacent, path P = p₁p₂p₃p₄, one further vertex v, and edges x₁x₂, x₁p₁, x₁p₂, x₁p₄, x₁v, x₂p₁, x₂p₃, x₂p₄, x₂v, p₁p₂, p₂p₃, p₃p₄. This graph is Berge (its only holes are three 4-holes, and it has no antihole), the vertex v is X-complete with no neighbour on P, and both disjuncts of the conclusion fail.
erratum.fix: The formalized 2.5 adds the hypothesis that X is anticonnected, matching the neighbouring theorems of §2. The single place the paper uses 2.5 is inside the proof of 2.8, where X is anticonnected, so nothing downstream is weakened.

highlights.prose: If G is recalcitrant then either G or G is bipartite. Clearly any counterexample to 1.3 is recalcitrant, so 13.5 will imply 1.3. On the other hand, for some future applications, it is desirable to keep closer track of which results hold under which hypotheses, instead of just using the blanket “recalcitrant” hypothesis. But at least, for the remainder of the paper we shall only be concerned with Berge graphs G such that in both G, G there is no appearance of K 4 and no long prism; that is, with the members of the class F5 introduced in section 1. Certainly every recalcitrant graph belongs to F 5 , by 10.6 and 9.7. erratum.title: Theorem 18.3, second conclusion: the parity clause fails for lines of length 1
erratum.problem: The second conclusion of 18.3 (p. 110) says that for every maximal subpath P′ of P with no Y-complete internal vertex, the length of P′ has the same parity as the number of ends of P′ in {p₁, pₙ} that are not Y-complete. A Y-complete edge pᵢpᵢ₊₁ of P is such a maximal subpath: it has no internal vertex, length 1, and no end in {p₁, pₙ} that fails to be Y-complete, so the clause demands 1 ≡ 0. Read literally the sentence therefore forces P to have no Y-complete edge, which contradicts the third conclusion of 18.3 and the paper's own use of it in 18.4 ("P contains an odd number of Y-complete edges"). The paper's proof carries the side condition "let P′ be a line of length ≥ 2", and its recap states the correct trichotomy including "either it has length 1"; the alternative was dropped when the recap became the statement.
erratum.fix: The formalized 18.3 adds the side condition 2 ≤ length of the subpath to the second conclusion, exactly the condition the printed proof uses. The only consumer, 18.5, applies the conclusion with index ≥ 3, so the paper's own uses are unaffected.

highlights.prose: First, a special case of the “2-join” due to Cornuéjols and Cunningham [13] — a proper 2-join in G is a partition (X 1 , X2 ) of V (G) such that there exist disjoint nonempty A i , Bi ⊆ Xi (i = 1, 2) satisfying: • every vertex of A1 is adjacent to every vertex of A2 , and every vertex of B1 is adjacent to every vertex of B2 , • there are no other edges between X1 and X2 , • for i = 1, 2, every component of G|Xi meets both Ai and Bi , and • for i = 1, 2, if |Ai | = |Bi | = 1 and G|Xi is a path joining the members of Ai and Bi , then it has odd length ≥ 3

Confidence lowered: the encoding restricts A1,A2 to V(G)\A and B1,B2 to V(G)\B, an argued interpretation rather than a literal transcription.
highlights.prose: Our second decomposition is a slight variation of the “homogeneous pair” of Chvátal and Sbihi [7] — a proper homogeneous pair in G is a pair of disjoint nonempty subsets (A, B) of V (G), such that, if A 1 , A2 respectively denote the sets of all A-complete vertices and all A-anticomplete vertices in V (G), and B 1 , B2 are defined similarly, then: • A1 ∪ A2 = B1 ∪ B2 = V (G) \ (A ∪ B) (and in particular, every vertex in A has a neighbour in B and a nonneighbour in B, and vice versa) • the four sets A1 ∩ B1 , A1 ∩ B2 , A2 ∩ B1 , A2 ∩ B2 are all nonempty

highlights.prose: The third kind of decomposition we use is due to Chvátal [6] — a skew partition in G is a partition (A, B) of V (G) such that A is not connected and B is not anticonnected

highlights.prose: Now we turn to a different type of subgraph, the double diamond. A double diamond means the graph with eight vertices a 1 , . . . , a4 , b1 , . . . , b4 and with the following adjacencies: every two a i ’s are adjacent except a3 a4 , every two bi ’s are adjacent except b3 b4 , and ai bi is an edge for 1 ≤ i ≤ 4

erratum.title: Theorem 9.3, outcome 4, is false as printed
erratum.problem: Outcome 4 asks for a vertex f ∈ F with the same neighbours as x₁ in V(P₁) ∪ V(P₂) ∪ V(Q₂) that is not adjacent to y₁. This can fail when Q₁ is long. Let H be the bipartite subdivision of K₄ whose two diagonals become branches of length 4 and 2, let G be the complement of the line graph L(H) on its 10 edges, and add one vertex f with exactly the neighbours of x₁. With the knot P₁ = a₁-b₁, P₂ = a₂-b₂, Q₁ = x₁-z₁-z₂-y₁, Q₂ = x₂-y₂ and F = {f}, every hypothesis of 9.3 holds (G is Berge; G and its complement have no K₄-enlargement appearance and no overshadowed K₄ appearance; the attachments of F are not local), yet all four outcomes fail. Outcome 4 fails because f is adjacent to y₁, exactly as x₁ is.
erratum.fix:
The formalized statement `thm_9_3` weakens the last clause of outcome 4 to "f has a non-neighbour on Q₁ other than x₁" (here z₁). The printed clause implies this one, and the two agree when Q₁ has length 1, so case (1) of the printed proof is untouched; case (2) and everything downstream, up to the main theorem, go through with the weaker outcome.

Lean checks that the four lists form a knot, that f is a twin of x₁, that all four printed outcomes fail, and that neither G nor its complement has a K₄-enlargement appearance, and bundles this as `printed_nine_three_false`.
